content: Now it turns out that for the last eight years, another major book was in the works: "W. E. B. Du Bois: Biography of a Race, 1868-1919" (Henry Holt & Company, New York, $35), a 735-page tome, described by Dr. Lewis in his preface as a project that "often rendered me unaware of the routine of daily life." Du Bois died in 1963 at the age of 95, and the research involved travel over three continents, inquiry into 28 archives and 99 library collections and interviews with more than 150 people. "And alas," Dr. Lewis said recently, "all this for what it turns out is only volume one." But "Du Bois" -- a candidate for the National Book Award in nonfiction -- is a powerfully thorough book that because its subject was such a extraordinary leader, so central to the political controversies around him, it compels a reappraisal of the post-Civil War era. Du Bois is perhaps best known in the civil rights movement for his insistence on full equality for his fellow blacks, as opposed to the accommodative policies of Booker T. Washington. But Dr. Lewis's book reveals much more about Du Bois as political strategist. In 1911, for example, when Woodrow Wilson, then Governor of New Jersey, prepared to enter the Presidential race, he asked Du Bois to influence blacks to depart from their traditional Republican stance and vote Democratic. After Wilson won with a larger-than-expected vote and segregationist politics continued, Du Bois retaliated with searing anti-Wilson editorials in The Crisis, the magazine of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People.

**Justification:** The passage discusses W.E.B. Du Bois's role as a political strategist, his advocacy for full equality for Black people, and his critiques of political figures and policies through his writings in *The Crisis*. This directly aligns with the definition of social and political advocacy, as it highlights his engagement in discourse and critique of social and political circumstances.

Nonetheless, there is something fortuitous in how Du Bois, writing from 1935, comments on and critiques the politics of history in 2022. The concluding chapter of “Black Reconstruction,” “The Propaganda of History,” is a polemical essay on the uses and abuses of historical narrative as well as a heated attack on the mainstream of American history writing as it existed in the 1920s and ’30s, when Du Bois’s book was conceived, researched and written. **Justification:** The passage discusses W.E.B. Du Bois's "Black Reconstruction in America" and its critique of historical narratives. But in this West African city, where streets are named for African states and for leaders of the African independence movement, Du Bois is revered as the father of Pan-Africanism. ''Du Bois still has great influence on us,'' Ghana's Foreign Minister, Obed Asamoah, said in an interview here. Ghana's Pan-Africanist foreign policy was evident last October, when the Government declared five days of mourning in honor of Samora M. Machel, the Mozambique leader who was killed in a plane crash in South Africa. Seeds of African Independence In the first half of this century, Du Bois organized five Pan-African congresses, meetings that planted the seeds for the crop of independent nations that sprang up in Africa in the 1960's. Almost a quarter of a century after Du Bois's death, the Pan-Africanist outlook can be seen in the joint pressure mounted by Africans and black Americans to win majority rule for South-West African, known as Namibia, and South Africa. Pan-Africanists have also encountered setbacks. For now, Du Bois's ideal of a United States of Africa seems far out of reach. One symbol of modern Africa's nationalist rivalries was Nigeria's abrupt expulsion - enforced with pistols and whips - of a million illegal workers from Ghana in 1983. The center, which is gathering his books, papers and other memorabilia, is in his bungalow on a quiet residential street here. The one-story Du Bois house has overhanging eaves to block the afternoon sun, ceiling fans to cool the interior and holes cut in closets to reduce mildew.

**Justification:** The passage explicitly discusses Du Bois's role in organizing Pan-African congresses, which are presented as foundational to the independence movements in Africa. It also highlights his ongoing influence on Ghana's foreign policy and the broader Pan-Africanist movement's efforts to achieve majority rule in South Africa, all of which fall under social and political advocacy.

Du Bois, who studied at the University of Berlin with some of the most acclaimed scholars of his day and who was the first Black American to receive a doctorate from Harvard, believed that history should aspire to be something like a science. And if that was to be the case, “if the record of human action is going to be set down with that accuracy and faithfulness of detail which will allow its use as a measuring rod and guidepost for the future of nations,” then in his view, “there must be set some standards of ethics in research and interpretation.” Du Bois’s view was that, when it came to Reconstruction and the “American Negro,” American historians had fallen far short of that ideal. Instead, they produced — for the consumption of both students and the general public — a history that cast Reconstruction as a “disgraceful attempt to subject white people to ignorant Negro rule.” Rather than treat history as “a science or as an art using the results of science,” they had used it as a tool of “pleasure and amusement, for inflating our national ego, and giving us a false but pleasurable sense of accomplishment.” This history, wrote Du Bois, existed only to “influence and educate the new generation along the way we wish,” where “we” meant the existing power structure.

**Justification:** The passage directly discusses Du Bois's critique of how American historians misrepresented the Reconstruction era, specifically concerning the "American Negro." It highlights his belief that history should be a science with ethical standards, and how historians failed this by creating a biased narrative that served to "inflate our national ego" and "influence and educate the new generation along the way we wish," which Du Bois saw as a distortion of truth for the benefit of the existing power structure. This clearly falls under the definition of social and political advocacy through historical critique.

In the early 19th century, Thomas Jefferson relied on elaborate mathematical equations to determine when a “mulatto” legally became a white person. Charles W. Chesnutt, a racially ambiguous writer, asked “What Is a White Man?” in an 1889 essay and poked fun at the laws that allowed a person to change his or her racial designation by walking across a state line. How was it possible, Chesnutt wondered, that the same person could be classified as black in North Carolina but white in South Carolina? Even W. E. B. Du Bois had trouble formulating a theoretically accurate account of racial identity, so he put it simply: A black man is “a person who must ride ‘Jim Crow’ in Georgia.” But his statement still leaves us with a puzzle: What would a black man be without Jim Crow to define him?

**Justification:** The passage discusses W.E.B. Du Bois's statement about racial identity and the impact of "Jim Crow" laws. The term “abolition-democracy” began with Du Bois and is worth further exploration. Abolition-democracy, Du Bois writes, was the “liberal movement among both laborers and small capitalists” who saw “the danger of slavery to both capital and labor.” Its standard-bearers were abolitionists like Wendell Phillips and radical antislavery politicians like Charles Sumner and Thaddeus Stevens, and in its eyes, “the only real object” of the Civil War was the abolition of slavery and “it was convinced that this could be thoroughly accomplished only if the emancipated Negroes became free citizens and voters.” It was also clear to some within abolition-democracy that “freedom in order to be free required a minimum of capital in addition to political rights.” In this way, abolition-democracy was an anticipation of social democratic ideology, although few of its proponents, in Du Bois’s view, grasped the full significance of their analysis of the relationship between political freedom, civil rights and economic security. Opposing abolition-democracy, in Du Bois’s telling, were the reactionaries of the former Confederate South who sought to “re-establish slavery by force.” The South, he writes, “opposed Negro education, opposed land and capital for Negroes, and violently and bitterly opposed any political power. It fought every conception inch by inch: no real emancipation, limited civil rights, no Negro schools, no votes for Negroes.” Between these two sides lay Northern industry and capital. It wanted profits and it would join whichever force enabled it to expand its power and reach. Initially, this meant abolition-democracy, as Northern industry feared the return of a South that might threaten its political and economic dominance. It “swung inevitably toward democracy” rather than allow the “continuation of Southern oligarchy,” Du Bois writes.

**Justification:** The passage directly discusses Du Bois's concept of "abolition-democracy," which he defined as a movement advocating for the abolition of slavery and the establishment of full citizenship and voting rights for emancipated Black people. It details the social and political goals of this movement, including the need for economic security, and contrasts it with the reactionary forces seeking to re-establish slavery. This clearly falls under the definition of social and political advocacy and critique of social problems.

Height, president of the National Council of Negro Women, rather than as fellow American citizens with problems. Her words echo the poignant "unasked question" of W. E. B. Du Bois, who wrote: "They approach me in a half-hesitant sort of way, eye me curiously or compassionately, and then instead of saying directly, How does it feel to be a problem? they say, I know an excellent colored man in my town. . . . Do not these Southern outrages make your blood boil? At these I smile, or am interested, or reduce the boiling to a simmer, as the occasion may require. To the real question, How does it feel to be a problem? I answer seldom a word." Nearly a century later, we confine discussions about race in America to the "problems" black people pose for whites rather than considering what this way of viewing black people reveals about us as a nation.

**Justification:** The passage directly quotes W.E.B. Du Bois's "unasked question" which critiques how Black people are perceived as a "problem." It also references Dorothy I.
